title: z0d1ak CTF
shortDescription: z0d1ak CTF is the flag-hunting competition run by z0d1ak, ACM-VIT's competitive CTF team - an open online Jeopardy qualifier followed by an onsite final at VIT Vellore for the twenty-five teams that make it through. Seven categories, a cash prize pool, and a field drawn from teams worldwide.
longDescription: z0d1ak CTF is the first competition z0d1ak has run rather than entered. The team spent its first two years climbing the CTFtime rankings against the likes of Shanghai Jiao Tong, Tokyo and Karlsruhe; z0d1ak CTF turns that experience around and puts ACM-VIT on the organising side of a globally open event.

The competition runs in two stages. The qualifier is online, Jeopardy-style and open to anyone: a 36-hour window across seven categories - forensics, reverse engineering, web exploitation, OSINT, cryptography, pwn and miscellaneous - hosted on the team's own rCTF deployment at ctf.z0d1ak.org. Challenges are written by the team, and the scoreboard runs live throughout.

The top twenty-five teams from the qualifier are invited to the finals, held in person at VIT Vellore over a single nine-hour session. Dataflow Security, the vulnerability research firm, came on as prize sponsor, with Hackviser, HackerDNA, HackingHub, CyberWarfare Labs and GenXYZ backing the prize table alongside them.

Beyond the podium, prizes reach down to twenty-fifth place, every team in the top twenty-five takes home a free .xyz domain, and six separate writeup prizes reward the clearest explanations of how a challenge fell.
format: Hybrid · Online Jeopardy qualifier into an onsite final
audience: Open to teams worldwide - the qualifier takes all comers
team: Teams · top 25 from the qualifier advance to the finals

tracks.name: Web Exploitation
tracks.description: Breaking web applications - injection, auth bypasses, logic flaws and everything that falls out of a badly trusted request.

tracks.name: Reverse Engineering
tracks.description: Pulling binaries apart to work out what they do and where the flag is hidden inside them.

tracks.name: PWN
tracks.description: Binary exploitation - memory corruption, control-flow hijacking and turning a crash into a shell.

tracks.name: Cryptography
tracks.description: Attacking broken schemes, weak parameters and misused primitives rather than brute-forcing them.

tracks.name: Forensics
tracks.description: Recovering what happened from disk images, packet captures, memory dumps and file carvings.

tracks.name: OSINT
tracks.description: Open-source intelligence - tracing a target through what has been left in public view.

tracks.name: Miscellaneous
tracks.description: The category for everything that refuses to sit in the others, including the occasional surprise format.

faq.a: The qualifier is open - any team, anywhere, no affiliation required. The finals are limited to the twenty-five teams that place highest in the qualifier.
In person at VIT Vellore, over a single nine-hour session. The qualifier before it is fully online.

faq.q: What categories should we prepare for?
faq.a: Seven: web exploitation, reverse engineering, pwn, cryptography, forensics, OSINT and miscellaneous.

faq.q: What platform does it run on?
faq.a: rCTF, self-hosted by the team at ctf.z0d1ak.org. Registration, challenges, the scoreboard and certificates all live there.

The category spread is deliberately wide, so there is something to solve at most levels, but it is scored as an open international CTF rather than a teaching event. If you are starting out, the team's CTF 101 writeup on the ACM-VIT blog is the better entry point.
z0d1ak, ACM-VIT's CTF team. The same team competes internationally year-round - their results and writeups are on the z0d1ak page.

pastEditions.description: The first edition, and the first competition ACM-VIT has run on the international CTF circuit rather than entered. The online qualifier ran 21-23 August across seven categories on the team's own rCTF deployment, drawing teams from well outside VIT; the twenty-five that came through it meet in person at VIT Vellore on 19 September for a nine-hour final. Dataflow Security backed the $1,750 cash prize pool as prize sponsor.
